edits.definition: Auxiliaries to trade are the support services that remove the hindrances which stand between a producer and a consumer, and so make trade itself possible. Transport removes the hindrance of place by carrying goods where they are demanded; warehousing removes the hindrance of time by storing goods until they are needed; insurance removes the hindrance of risk by covering loss from fire, theft or accident; banking removes the hindrance of finance by providing credit and payment mechanisms; and advertising removes the hindrance of information by telling buyers what is available. None of these services produces goods itself, yet industry and trade depend on all of them, which is why they are treated as part of business activity.

Business risk is the possibility that a business will earn inadequate profit or even suffer loss because of uncertainties and unforeseen events. It arises from two broad classes of causes: internal factors within the firm's control, such as a strike, a machine failure or fraud by an employee, and external factors beyond its control, such as a change in government policy, a rise in input prices, new competition or a natural calamity. Business risk is unavoidable in any genuine enterprise — the saying 'no risk, no gain' expresses this — and its degree varies with the nature and size of the business; profit is conventionally treated as the reward the owner earns for bearing it.

Sole proprietorship is the form of business organisation in which one person owns, manages and controls the entire enterprise, supplies the capital (or borrows in their own name), receives all the profits and bears all the losses and risks. The owner and the business have no separate legal existence: the firm's debts are the owner's debts, and liability is unlimited, extending to personal property. Formation and closure are simple and require little legal formality, the owner enjoys complete decision-making freedom and secrecy, and the business enjoys no continuity independent of the owner — incapacity or death can end it. It suits enterprises needing quick decisions, personal touch and small capital.

Outsourcing is the practice of contracting out a business activity to an external specialist agency instead of performing it with the firm's own staff, so that the firm concentrates its resources on the activities where it holds its core competence. Typical outsourced work includes routine and support services such as housekeeping, security, payroll processing, customer care, advertising, legal services and, in the Indian experience, large-scale business process outsourcing (BPO) and knowledge process work for clients abroad. Its benefits are lower cost, access to expertise and technology, flexibility to scale with demand and sharper focus on strategy; its risks include loss of direct control, dependence on the provider, confidentiality concerns and resistance from employees whose work is transferred.

Social responsibility of business is the obligation of a business enterprise to act in ways that serve the objectives and values of society — not only to obey the law but to weigh the effects of its decisions on every group affected by it: owners, employees, consumers, suppliers, the local community, government and the environment. It rests on the justification that business uses society's resources, exists by public consent, and is best served in the long run by public well-being. Responsibility extends from legal responsibility (compulsory compliance) through economic responsibility (producing goods profitably) to ethical and discretionary responsibilities, such as honest advertising, fair dealing and environmental care, which business undertakes voluntarily.

Business ethics are the moral principles and standards — honesty, fairness, integrity, promise-keeping, respect for others — that guide behaviour in the world of business, distinguishing right conduct from merely profitable or legally permissible conduct. Their importance in modern business follows from the conditions in which firms now operate: consumers and media scrutinise corporate conduct, law and regulation reach deeper into enterprise behaviour, and a firm's reputation travels instantly in a connected world. Ethics in practice means truthful advertising, fair pricing, safe products, non-discriminatory employment, payment of due taxes and protection of the environment. Firms that institutionalise ethics — codes of conduct, ethics committees, example from the top — win employee commitment and public trust that no advertising can buy.

A promoter is the person who conceives the idea of forming a company, takes the necessary steps to give it legal existence, and carries the responsibility for the enterprise until the company comes into being and its management passes to the board of directors. The promoter's work spans discovering the business opportunity, detailed investigation of its feasibility, assembling the subscribers and finances, preparing and getting signed the memorandum and articles of association, and completing the registration formalities with the Registrar of Companies. Legally the promoter stands in a fiduciary position towards the company: any profit made secretly must be accounted for, and contracts made before incorporation (preliminary contracts) do not bind the company automatically.

Export-import documentation is the complete set of commercial, regulatory and financial papers that must accompany international trade transactions, because the goods pass through two customs territories and the parties deal across currencies and legal systems. The commercial documents include the proforma and sales invoice, packing list and certificate of origin; the regulatory documents include shipping bill (for export) and bill of entry (for import), the IEC code and bill of lading or airway bill; the financial documents include the letter of credit, bill of exchange and insurance policy. Each document serves a purpose — transfer of title, claim of export incentives, customs clearance or payment settlement — and a single error can delay cargo or block payment.

The importance of management lies in its role as the force that makes group effort effective. It helps in achieving group goals by directing individual effort towards the objectives of the organisation; it increases efficiency by reducing cost through better planning, organising and controlling of resources; it creates a dynamic organisation that adapts to a changing environment instead of clinging to old methods; it helps in achieving personal objectives by developing people and matching work to their needs; and it contributes to the development of society by supplying quality goods, generating employment and adopting new technology. Where resources are limited and goals are shared, management is what converts scattered effort into achievement.

The technological environment comprises the forces that develop new techniques, products and processes of doing things: scientific improvements and innovations in production, automation and robotics, information technology and digital platforms, communication networks, new materials, and the research and development activity of firms and institutions. It is among the most dramatic elements of the business environment because it alters what is produced, how it is produced and how it is sold — e-commerce and digital payments redraw marketing, mechanisation redraws agriculture and manufacturing. Technology creates opportunity and threat together: firms that adopt early gain cost and quality advantages, while those that delay become uncompetitive.

Opportunities and threats analysis is the systematic scanning of the external business environment to identify favourable trends a firm can exploit (opportunities) and unfavourable trends it must defend against (threats). Opportunities arise from growing markets, technological change, favourable government policy, rising incomes or the exit of competitors; threats come from new entrants, substitute products, changing consumer tastes, adverse regulation, resource shortages and competition. The analysis converts environmental scanning into strategy: each opportunity is weighed for its fit with the firm's strengths, each threat for its severity and probability, so that plans can be made before events force them. It is the external half of SWOT analysis, to be read together with the internal strengths-weaknesses study.

Staffing is the managerial function of filling, and keeping filled, all positions in the organisation structure. Its cycle runs from estimating human resource requirements (how many people, with what skills), through recruitment (searching for suitable candidates), selection (choosing among them through tests and interviews), placement and orientation (putting the right person in the right job and introducing them to the organisation), to training and development (improving competence for present and future jobs), performance appraisal (judging how well each person performs), and promotion, transfer and compensation decisions. Staffing is a continuous process because people leave, retire and must be developed, and it is entrusted to both the personnel department and every manager who supervises people.

Performance appraisal is the systematic evaluation of an employee's present job performance and potential for growth, made against predetermined standards and communicated to the employee as feedback. A sound appraisal uses clear, job-related criteria and methods ranging from traditional ranking and rating scales to modern tools such as MBO (appraisal against jointly set objectives) and 360-degree appraisal (feedback from superiors, peers, subordinates and customers). Its purposes are administrative — decisions on promotions, transfers, increments and terminations — and developmental — identifying training needs, counselling and motivating employees. Done fairly it strengthens trust and performance; done carelessly it breeds grievances, which is why training of appraisers and objectivity of standards matter.

Directing is the managerial function of instructing, guiding, motivating, communicating with and leading people so that they act willingly and effectively towards organisational objectives. It is called the heart of management-in-action because planning and organising remain paper work until directing initiates actual performance. Its elements are supervision (overseeing the work of subordinates), motivation (arousing the will to work by satisfying needs and incentives), leadership (influencing people so they follow voluntarily) and communication (the two-way exchange of facts and ideas that keeps everyone informed). Directing flows from top to bottom through the hierarchy, operates at every level of management, is a continuous activity, and treats each employee as a distinct individual rather than a mere factor of production.

Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, facts, opinions, information and feelings between two or more persons so as to create common understanding. Its cycle contains the sender, who initiates; the message, the content of the exchange; encoding, the conversion of the idea into transmittable symbols; the media or channel that carries it; decoding, the receiver's translation of the symbols back into meaning; the receiver, to whom it is addressed; feedback, the receiver's response that completes the loop; and noise — any barrier of language, status, distraction or distortion that interferes at any stage. Effective communication is judged not by what is sent but by what is understood, and it flows formally through the organisational structure and informally alongside it.

Leadership is the art of influencing the behaviour of people so that they strive willingly and enthusiastically towards the achievement of group goals. It is an interpersonal process between the leader and followers, resting on guidance, motivation and example rather than on formal authority: a leader may be appointed, but leadership exists only while people choose to follow. The elements are the leader, the followers, the situation and communication among them, with styles ranging from autocratic through democratic (participative) to laissez-faire, chosen by the task and the people. Good leadership builds confidence, provides vision and initiative, raises morale and develops followers into future leaders — a manager who cannot lead secures compliance at best, never commitment.

Controlling is the managerial function of comparing actual performance with the standards set during planning, finding deviations, and taking corrective action so that objectives are achieved. Its process has defined steps: setting performance standards (in quantity, cost, time or quality), measuring actual performance, comparing the two and analysing significant deviations (through management by exception, so attention falls on what matters), and finally corrective action — which may mean fixing the operation or, where the standard itself was wrong, revising the standard. Controlling is a forward-looking function (lessons feed future plans) and it completes the planning-control loop, since planning without control is meaningless and control without planning is blind.

Marketing research is the systematic and objective process of gathering, recording, analysing and interpreting data about marketing problems — consumers, products, prices, channels, promotion and competition — to help marketing decisions. Its steps run from defining the problem and research objectives, through developing the research design, choosing primary sources (surveys, observation, experiments) or secondary sources (published data), collecting the information, analysing it with appropriate tools, to reporting findings and their limitations for managerial use. Distinct from market research (which centres on the market for a specific product), marketing research covers the entire marketing activity; its value lies in reducing the uncertainty under which products are designed, priced and launched.
